title: TypeScript collections versus C# generics collections
hook: TypeScript arrays and Map/Set erase at compile time — C# List<T> and Dictionary<K,V> enforce generics at runtime through the CLR. Knowing where types disappear prevents false confidence at JSON and API boundaries.

blocks.text: TypeScript collection types (`T[]`, `Map<K,V>`, `Set<T>`) describe **compile-time** shapes only — emitted JavaScript uses plain Array and ES2015 Map/Set with no generic metadata. C# **List<T>**, **Dictionary<K,V>**, **HashSet<T>**, and **IReadOnlyList<T>** carry runtime type information via generics, with **where** constraints on keys and values. TypeScript uses **structural typing** — if it looks like an array, it is `T[]`. C# uses **nominal typing** — only declared implementations satisfy interfaces.

entries.plainDefinition: TS generics vanish on emit — no T at runtime.
C# runtime retains type args — List<int> vs List<string> are different types.
TS matches by shape — duck typing at compile time.
entries.example: { length: number } usable where array-like expected

entries.plainDefinition: C# read-only collection interface with runtime wrapper.

blocks.text: C# developers moving to TypeScript often assume `List<User>` safety extends to runtime — it does not. `JSON.parse` returns `any` or `unknown`, not `User[]`. `fetch` does not deserialize to `Dictionary`. Interop between .NET APIs and TS frontends requires explicit validation (Zod, manual guards). Senior interviews compare covariance (`IReadOnlyList` vs `readonly T[]`), nullability (`T?` vs `T | undefined`), and when to mirror C# patterns with TS utility types.

blocks.title: Boundary rule
blocks.body: TS types end at the wire — validate JSON into typed collections at every API boundary.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: List<T> → T[]
items.body: Dynamic array — same amortized O(1) push.

items.title: Dictionary<K,V> → Map<K,V> or Record
items.body: Map for any keys; Record for string JSON keys.

items.title: IReadOnlyList<T> → readonly T[]
items.body: Compile-time only in TS — no runtime wrapper.

snippet.label: JSON boundary — types do not survive wire
snippet.explanation: C# Web API might return List<UserDto> with runtime type — TS fetch gets unknown JSON. Must validate each element into User[].

snippet.label: Dictionary vs Map interop
snippet.explanation: JSON objects map to Record<string, T> in TS. C# Dictionary string keys deserialize to plain object — not Map instance.

snippet.label: readonly vs IReadOnlyList semantics
snippet.explanation: TS readonly is not a runtime guard. C# IReadOnlyList wrapper can enforce on mutation attempts.

snippet.label: Failure mode — trusting API generic type
snippet.explanation: as OrderDto provides zero runtime safety. Same mistake as casting dynamic in C# without validation.

blocks.title: Assuming deserialized JSON is typed
blocks.body: List<User> in OpenAPI docs does not make fetch return User[] — validate.

blocks.title: Record for object-keyed Map
blocks.body: C# reference-type keys need Map in TS — Record only supports string | number | symbol keys as properties.

blocks.text: OpenAPI/Swagger codegen generates TS interfaces — still no runtime guarantee unless paired with validators. C# source generators and TS satisfy different layers. For shared DTOs in monorepos, consider JSON Schema or protobuf as the contract. Covariance: C# IEnumerable<out T> vs TS readonly array covariance. Performance: C# Span<T> has no TS equivalent — use TypedArray for numeric buffers.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Believing TS generics exist at runtime. Casting fetch.json() to interface. Cannot map Dictionary/List/HashSet to TS equivalents.

interviewTakeaways: TS collection generics erase — CLR keeps them at runtime.
JSON boundaries need validation — types do not cross the wire.
60s: TS types are compile-time contracts on JS runtime collections. C# enforces at CLR. Always validate API JSON. readonly ≠ IReadOnlyList runtime guard.
Follow-up: OpenAPI codegen limits, Zod at boundaries, covariance comparison.
commonPitfalls: Weak: "TypeScript List<T> like C#" — no runtime List type.
Strong: "Generics erase on emit. Validate unknown into T[]. Map C# collections to TS equivalents by behavior not runtime type."

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS JSON.parse returns plain objects/arrays — TS types are annotations only unless validated.
C# List<T> is a runtime generic type with capacity semantics; TS T[] is a compile-time view over JS Array.
